claim: MHCI H2-Kb/H2-Db double knockout (KbDb−/−) mice exhibit enhanced associative LTD at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD).
source: In the cerebellum, classical MHCI H2-Kb (H2-Kb) and MHCI H2-Db (H2-Db) are highly expressed in Purkinje cells, and double-knockout mice, MHCI H2-Kb/H2-Db−/− (KbDb−/−; Vugmeyster et al., 1998; Schott et al., 2003; referred to as double knockout (DKO) here), exhibit enhanced associative LTD at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD) (McConnell et al. 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McConnell et al. 2009, which provides experimental evidence for enhanced pf-Pk LTD in DKO mice.

claim: DKO mice were significantly impaired in learning to increase the amplitude of the VOR when training was done using 1 Hz visual-vestibular stimuli.
source: DKO mice were significantly impaired in learning to increase the amplitude of the VOR when training was done using 1 Hz visual-vestibular stimuli (Figure 1D, solid bars; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and associated source data, demonstrating impaired VOR-increase learning in DKO mice at 1 Hz training frequency.

claim: There was no significant impairment of learning to increase the VOR when training was done with lower frequency visual-vestibular stimuli of 0.6 Hz in DKO mice.
source: However, as previously reported in LTD-impaired mice (Boyden et al., 2006; Schonewille et al., 2011), there was no significant impairment of learning to increase the VOR when training was done with lower frequency visual-vestibular stimuli of 0.6 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, top)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies showing similar frequency-dependent effects.

claim: DKO mice showed no significant impairment in learning to decrease the VOR at either 0.6 Hz or 1.0 Hz training frequency.
source: or when learning to decrease the VOR at either training frequency (Figure 1E, solid bars, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Baseline performance of the VOR and visually-driven oculomotor behaviors were indistinguishable between DKO and WT mice.
source: Baseline performance of the VOR and visually-driven oculomotor behaviors were indistinguishable between DKO and WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3), suggesting an impairment of the learning mechanism itself, rather than other sensory or motor deficits.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3, demonstrating no baseline differences in VOR and oculomotor behaviors.

claim: The impaired learning phenotype in DKO mice could be attributed to the loss of H2-Db expression in Purkinje cells.
source: The impaired learning phenotype in DKO mice could be attributed to the loss of H2-Db expression in Purkinje cells, the post-synaptic site of pf-Pk LTD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known role of Purkinje cells as the post-synaptic site of pf-Pk LTD and subsequent rescue experiments.

claim: Virally-mediated rescue of H2-Db expression specifically in Purkinje cells of the flocculus of adult global DKO mice was sufficient to rescue their impaired VOR-increase learning.
source: Although H2-Kb and H2-Db expression is not exclusive to the cerebellar Purkinje cells, virally-mediated rescue of H2-Db expression specifically in Purkinje cells of the flocculus (Figure 1A–C), the cerebellar region necessary for VOR learning, of adult global DKO mice, was sufficient to rescue their impaired VOR-increase learning (Figure 1D, hatched bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of the learning deficit after viral expression of H2-Db in Purkinje cells, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rescue of H2-Db expression in adult neurons can restore normal function, even in animals that developed in the absence of this molecule.
source: Thus, rescue of H2-Db expression in adult neurons can restore normal function, even in animals that developed in the absence of this molecule, indicating that the role of MHCI molecules is not confined to the developing nervous system, but actively regulates plasticity in adults as well.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment showing that adult viral expression of H2-Db restores normal learning.

claim: Expression of H2-Db had no effect on VOR-decrease learning.
source: Expression of H2-Db had no effect on VOR-decrease learning (Figure 1E, hatched bars), which is insensitive to perturbations of pf-Pk LTD (Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006; Schonewille et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous studies showing VOR-decrease learning is insensitive to pf-Pk LTD perturbations.

claim: The lower induction threshold for pf-Pk LTD in the DKO mice could allow normal basal activity in the circuit to aberrantly recruit LTD and deplete the pool of LTD-eligible synapses.
source: In particular, the lower induction threshold for pf-Pk LTD in the DKO mice (McConnell et al. 2009) could allow normal basal activity in the circuit to aberrantly recruit LTD and deplete the pool of LTD-eligible synapses.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the known lower threshold for LTD in DKO mice and the observed learning impairment.

claim: The capacity for LTD could be exhausted (saturated) even before the start of training in DKO mice, rendering the circuit unable to support new learning that depends on pf-Pk LTD.
source: Thus, the capacity for LTD could be exhausted, i.e., saturated, even before the start of training, rendering the circuit unable to support new learning that depends on pf-Pk LTD (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis (saturation hypothesis) proposed to explain the observed learning impairment in DKO mice.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of climbing fibers for 30 min in WT mice blocked subsequent VOR-increase learning.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of climbing fibers for 30 min, to induce pf-Pk LTD in the flocculus of WT mice, blocked subsequent VOR-increase learning (solid cyan trace; *p=0.03, F(1,10) = 5.912, two-factor repeated measures ANOVA, CF stim n = 6, Sham n = 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that climbing fiber stimulation impaired VOR-increase learning, with statistical significance reported.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation had no effect on VOR-decrease learning in WT mice.
source: but had no effect on VOR-decrease learning (dashed cyan trace; n.s. p=0.68, F(1,5) = 0.20) relative to sham stimulation controls in animals that did not express ChR2 in the climbing fibers (black).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant effect of climbing fiber stimulation on VOR-decrease learning.

claim: Non-specific LTD-induction procedure via optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation did not affect the amplitude of the VOR.
source: This non-specific LTD-induction procedure did not affect the amplitude of the VOR, measured after climbing fiber stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The normal baseline VOR amplitude in DKO mice is consistent with non-specific LTD not affecting VOR amplitude.
source: This is consistent with the normal baseline VOR amplitude in DKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and in wild type mice after lesions of the flocculus (Rambold et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Katoh et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and citations to previous studies showing similar results.

claim: Non-specific manipulations of the flocculus are not sufficient to have a coordinated effect on the VOR behavior.
source: Together, these observations indicate that non-specific manipulations of the flocculus are not sufficient to have a coordinated effect on the VOR behavior, and that LTD only increases the amplitude of the VOR if it is induced selectively in the appropriate subset of pf-Pk synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations including climbing fiber stimulation, baseline VOR in DKO mice, and lesion studies.

claim: If non-specific LTD depleted the pool of LTD-eligible synapses, it could impair subsequent LTD-dependent learning.
source: Nevertheless, if non-specific LTD depleted the pool of LTD-eligible synapses, it could impair subsequent LTD-dependent learning (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference about the mechanism by which non-specific LTD could impair learning.

claim: VOR-increase learning was impaired after climbing fiber stimulation in WT mice.
source: Accordingly, VOR-increase learning was impaired after climbing fiber stimulation (Figure 2B, CF Stim, cyan vs. Sham Stim, black; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B comparing climbing fiber stimulation to sham stimulation.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation before training did not perturb subsequent VOR-decrease learning.
source: Notably, climbing fiber stimulation before training did not perturb subsequent VOR-decrease learning, which also relies on the cerebellar flocculus (Koekkoek et al., 1997; Rambold et al., 2002) but is insensitive to disruptions of pf-Pk LTD (Boyden et al., 2006) (Figure 2B, dashed traces).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous studies showing VOR-decrease learning is insensitive to pf-Pk LTD disruptions.

claim: The specificity of the learning impairment in WT mice after climbing fiber stimulation indicates that elevated levels of pf-Pk LTD prior to training can produce a phenotype like that observed in the DKO mice.
source: The specificity of the learning impairment in WT mice after climbing fiber stimulation indicates that elevated levels of pf-Pk LTD prior to training can produce a phenotype like that observed in the DKO mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of the learning impairment phenotype between climbing fiber-stimulated WT mice and DKO mice.

claim: Pf-Pk LTD can be actively reversed by post-synaptic LTP of the same synapses.
source: Pf-Pk LTD can be actively reversed by post-synaptic LTP of the same synapses (Lev-Ram et al., 2003), providing a cellular mechanism for reversing LTD saturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lev-Ram et al., 2003, which provides experimental evidence for LTP-mediated reversal of LTD.

claim: Behavioral VOR-decrease training has been shown to rapidly reverse any evidence of prior VOR-increase learning.
source: Moreover, behavioral VOR-decrease training has been shown to rapidly reverse any evidence of prior VOR-increase learning (Boyden and Raymond, 2003), suggesting that it rapidly reverses any pf-Pk LTD or other plasticity induced during VOR-increase learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boyden and Raymond, 2003, which provides experimental evidence for behavioral reversal of VOR-increase learning.

claim: VOR-decrease pre-training significantly enhanced subsequent VOR-increase learning in DKO mice relative to DKO mice that did not receive the pre-training.
source: In the DKO mice, this pre-training significantly enhanced subsequent VOR-increase learning relative to DKO mice that did not receive the pre-training (Figure 3A, compare red traces and bars in middle vs. left panels; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A comparing DKO mice with and without pre-training.

claim: VOR-decrease pre-training had the opposite effect on WT mice, impairing subsequent VOR-increase learning.
source: Notably, pre-training had the opposite effect on WT mice, impairing subsequent VOR-increase learning (Figure 3A, compare black traces in middle vs. left panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A comparing WT mice with and without pre-training.

claim: After VOR-decrease pre-training, DKO mice learned better than WT mice during subsequent VOR-increase training.
source: Since the pre-training enhanced learning in the DKO mice, but impaired learning in the WT mice, the DKO mice learned better than the WT after pre-training. Hence, the pre-training not only reversed the learning impairment, but also revealed a capacity for enhanced learning in the DKO mice relative to WT mice (Figure 3A, compare black vs. red traces in middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A comparing DKO and WT mice after pre-training.

claim: Pre-training with a vestibular stimulus alone did not improve subsequent VOR-increase learning in the DKO mice relative to WT mice.
source: Also, the enhanced learning was unmasked specifically by pre-training with the associative VOR-decrease training paradigm, which paired visual and vestibular stimuli. Simply decreasing the VOR amplitude with a non-associative, habituation paradigm, which presented the vestibular stimulus alone, was not sufficient to unmask the enhanced learning (Figure 3A, right, Vestibular Only Pre-training).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A comparing associative VOR-decrease pre-training to vestibular-only pre-training.

claim: Only the appropriate pre-training experience can put the circuit of the DKO mice into a state that enables their enhanced synaptic plasticity to support enhanced learning.
source: Thus, only the appropriate pre-training experience can put the circuit of the DKO mice into a state that enables their enhanced synaptic plasticity to support enhanced learning (Figure 2A, orange arrow).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that only associative VOR-decrease pre-training, not vestibular-only pre-training, enhanced learning in DKO mice.

claim: The enhanced learning phenotype in DKO mice was only observed when training was done using high-frequency (1.0 Hz) visual-vestibular stimuli, but not at 0.6 Hz.
source: First, the enhanced learning phenotype, like the impaired learning phenotype (Figure 1D, solid bars, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, top), was only observed when training was done using high-frequency (1.0 Hz) visual-vestibular stimuli (Figure 3A, middle panel), but not a slightly lower stimulus frequency of 0.6 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 comparing learning at different stimulus frequencies.

claim: The enhanced learning phenotype reverted to WT phenotype after virally-mediated expression of H2-Db in the Purkinje cells of adult DKO mice.
source: In addition, the enhanced learning phenotype, like the impaired learning phenotype in the DKO mice, reverted to WT phenotype after virally-mediated expression of H2-Db in the Purkinje cells of adult DKO mice (compare Figure 3B, left panel, with Figure 3A, middle panel, and Figure 1D, hatched bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B comparing DKO mice with H2-Db rescue to those without.

claim: Both the enhanced and impaired learning phenotypes of DKO mice share a common mechanism, involving the same set of synapses.
source: The commonality of these features suggests that both the enhanced and impaired learning phenotypes of DKO mice share a common mechanism, involving the same set of synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similar frequency dependence and rescue by H2-Db expression for both enhanced and impaired learning phenotypes.

claim: Classical models of synaptic plasticity did not reproduce the observation of impaired learning with enhanced plasticity.
source: Classical models of LTP and LTD did not reproduce our observation of impaired learning with enhanced plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results showing that classical models fail to account for the experimental observations.

claim: A binary synapse model and a generalized linear multistate model incorrectly predict that enhanced plasticity would enhance VOR-increase learning.
source: We tested a simple binary synapse model (Figure 4B), and a more generalized linear multistate model with multiple synaptic strengths (see Appendix). These models encapsulate classical notions of synaptic plasticity as straightforward changes in synaptic strength, to a maximal or minimal bound. However, one can show mathematically, that for all values of the parameters of these models, the enhanced intrinsic LTD rate dominates the saturation effect, at least for the initial phase of learning. Thus, these models incorrectly predict that enhanced plasticity would enhance VOR-increase learning (Figure 4B, solid red vs. black trace, green bracket; see Appendix for an analytical solution and predictions of models for longer time scales).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results and mathematical analysis showing that classical models fail to predict impaired learning with enhanced plasticity.

claim: A serial model with only two different synaptic weights, but with each weight associated with multiple internal states, can account for the impaired learning phenotype in the DKO mice.
source: One model that possesses both essential properties of amplified saturation effects and stubborn synaptic states is a serial model (Leibold and Kempter 2008; Ben Dayan Rubin and Fusi, 2007) with only two different synaptic weights, but with each weight associated with multiple, internal states (Figure 4D). Enhancing LTD in these models leads to an exponential distribution over synaptic states, which strongly depletes the pool of synapses available to express LTD. This exponential distribution of synapses (Figure 4D, top right) can account for the impaired learning phenotype in the DKO mice by providing sufficient depletion of LTD-eligible synapses by spontaneous basal activity to overwhelm the higher intrinsic LTD rate in the remaining LTD-eligible synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that a serial model can reproduce the observed impaired learning phenotype.

claim: In the serial model, pre-training in the DKO mice reversed the saturation bias, allowing the higher intrinsic LTD rate to dominate.
source: In this model, pre-training in the DKO mice reversed this saturation bias (Figure 4D, bottom right vs. top right), allowing the higher intrinsic LTD rate to dominate.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing how pre-training affects the distribution of synaptic states in the serial model.

claim: In the serial model, pre-training in WT mice pushed synapses deep into the chain of potentiated states, thereby reducing their ability to undergo a subsequent transition to a depressed state.
source: In contrast, WT mice started with many LTD-eligible synapses, but pre-training pushed synapses deep into the chain of potentiated states, thereby reducing their ability to undergo a subsequent transition to a depressed state (Figure 4D, bottom left, orange bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing how pre-training affects the distribution of synaptic states in WT mice in the serial model.

claim: The model predicts that with extended VOR-increase training, the advantage conferred on the DKO mice relative to WT mice by pre-training should disappear.
source: Notably, the model predicts that with extended VOR-increase training, the advantage conferred on the DKO mice relative to WT mice by pre-training should disappear (see Appendix).
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the computational model about the effects of extended training.

claim: Models with metaplasticity, where the capacity for a synaptic weight to change depends on the history of prior plasticity events, could account for the empirical observations.
source: Other synaptic models in which the capacity for a synaptic weight to change depends on the history of prior plasticity events could also account for our empirical observations. Models with such metaplasticity include the cascade model (Fusi et al., 2005) (see Appendix), and a multistate model with multiple synaptic strengths and lower transition probabilities for the deeper states (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that models with history-dependent plasticity can reproduce the experimental observations.

claim: Under conditions where the recent activity leaves many synapses of WT mice in the labile, LTD-eligible states, enhancing plasticity tends to push the synapses out of these LTD-eligible states before training and thus impairs learning despite enhanced plasticity.
source: In essence, under conditions where the recent activity leaves many synapses of WT mice in the labile, LTD-eligible states, enhancing plasticity tends to push the synapses out of these LTD-eligible states before training and thus impairs learning despite enhanced plasticity (compare Figure 4D, top-left with top-right).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results about how enhanced plasticity affects synaptic states.

claim: A history-dependent alteration in the capacity to undergo additional plasticity has been documented experimentally at some synapses in the hippocampus.
source: A history-dependent alteration in the capacity to undergo additional plasticity has been documented experimentally at some synapses in the hippocampus (Montgomery and Madison, 2002; Petersen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies in the hippocampus.

claim: History-dependence in the plasticity of cerebellar synapses, required by the model to explain the observed behavioral phenotypes, constitutes a key prediction that can be tested in future empirical investigations of the synaptic physiology.
source: Such history-dependence in the plasticity of cerebellar synapses, required by our model to explain our observed behavioral phenotypes, constitutes a key prediction that can be tested in future empirical investigations of the synaptic physiology.
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the computational model about a property of cerebellar synapses that should be tested experimentally.

claim: The same individual animals with enhanced plasticity can respond to the same behavioral training with either enhanced or impaired learning, depending on the recent history of experience.
source: Here, we established that the same individual animals with enhanced plasticity can respond to the same behavioral training with either enhanced or impaired learning, depending on the recent history of experience.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing that DKO mice exhibit either impaired or enhanced learning depending on whether they received pre-training.

claim: The capacity for new learning is determined by a dynamic interplay between the threshold for synaptic plasticity and the recent history of activity.
source: Thus, the capacity for new learning is determined by a dynamic interplay between the threshold for synaptic plasticity and the recent history of activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results showing how plasticity threshold and activity history interact to determine learning outcomes.

claim: Classical models of synaptic plasticity, in which an LTP event simply increases the synaptic strength and an LTD event simply decreases the synaptic strength, do not readily explain the behavioral data.
source: Classical models of synaptic plasticity, in which an LTP event simply increases the synaptic strength and an LTD event simply decreases the synaptic strength, do not readily explain our behavioral data.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that classical models fail to reproduce the experimental observations.

claim: In classical models, enhancing plasticity led to enhanced learning, across the entire parameter space, and independent of the history of previous learning experiences.
source: We showed that in such models, enhancing plasticity led to enhanced learning, across the entire parameter space, and independent of the history of previous learning experiences.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results and mathematical analysis of classical models.

claim: A critical theoretical ingredient required to account for the data is a history-dependent form of synaptic plasticity in which repeated LTD changes the internal state of the synapse into a less labile state.
source: A critical, theoretical ingredient required to account for our data is a history-dependent form of synaptic plasticity (Montgomery and Madison, 2002; Petersen et al., 1998; Fusi et al., 2005) in which repeated LTD changes the internal state of the synapse into a less labile state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results and citations to previous theoretical and experimental work on history-dependent plasticity.

claim: Enhanced LTD can deplete the pool of labile synapses capable of supporting further learning, leading to impaired learning despite enhanced plasticity.
source: Then enhanced LTD can deplete the pool of labile synapses capable of supporting further learning, leading to impaired learning despite enhanced plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results about the mechanism by which enhanced plasticity can impair learning.

claim: The similar learning deficits in mice with enhanced pf-Pk LTD and impaired pf-Pk LTD could reflect a similar underlying cause, namely the unavailability of pf-Pk LTD during training.
source: Thus, the similar learning deficits in mice with enhanced pf-Pk LTD (Figure 1D) and impaired pf-Pk LTD (Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006) could reflect a similar underlying cause, namely the unavailability of pf-Pk LTD during training (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of learning deficits in mice with opposite manipulations of pf-Pk LTD and the saturation hypothesis.

claim: Impairments of learning due to enhanced plasticity have generally been attributed to an over-recruitment of the enhanced plasticity mechanism at inappropriate synapses during training corrupting the memory trace.
source: Such impairments have generally been attributed to an over-recruitment of the enhanced plasticity mechanism at inappropriate synapses during training corrupting the memory trace (Migaud et al., 1998; Koekkoek et al., 2005; Martin et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this mechanism for impaired learning with enhanced plasticity.

claim: The results raise the alternative possibility that enhancing the plasticity mechanism necessary for learning might lead to its under-recruitment at appropriate synapses during learning, as a result of saturation.
source: Our results raise the alternative possibility that enhancing the plasticity mechanism necessary for learning might lead, instead to its under-recruitment at appropriate synapses during learning, as a result of saturation (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental and modeling results, proposing an alternative mechanism for impaired learning with enhanced plasticity.

claim: Behavioral training paradigms that induce learning can occlude the subsequent induction of synaptic plasticity in brain slices.
source: Behavioral training paradigms that induce learning can occlude the subsequent induction of synaptic plasticity in brain slices (Schreurs et al., 1997; Pascoli et al., 2012; Rioult-Pedotti et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies showing occlusion of plasticity after behavioral training.

claim: Strong, artificial stimulation of neural activity in vivo to saturate a plasticity mechanism has been shown to impair subsequent learning in animals with normal synaptic plasticity.
source: and strong, artificial stimulation of neural activity in vivo to saturate a plasticity mechanism has been shown to impair subsequent learning in animals with normal synaptic plasticity (Martin et al., 2000; Moser et al., 1998), as we found for cerebellar climbing fiber stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the experimental results from climbing fiber stimulation in the current study.

claim: Saturation has not been identified previously as a factor that could limit the ability of enhanced synaptic plasticity to enhance learning.
source: Despite its consideration in these contexts, saturation has not been identified previously as a factor that could limit the ability of enhanced synaptic plasticity to enhance learning.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature and the novelty of the current findings.

claim: In mice with a low threshold for associative synaptic plasticity, saturation of the plasticity and occlusion of further learning may occur in response to the normal, ongoing, basal levels of activity in a circuit, in the absence of any training or neural stimulation.
source: In particular, our results suggest that in mice with a low threshold for associative synaptic plasticity, saturation of the plasticity and occlusion of further learning may occur, not only in response to the patterns of elevated neural activity that can induce saturation in WT animals, but also in response to the normal, ongoing, basal levels of activity in a circuit, in the absence of any training or neural stimulation (compare Figure 1D and Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing DKO mice without stimulation to WT mice with climbing fiber stimulation.

claim: Enhanced synaptic plasticity, in the form of a lower threshold for induction, can be opposed by a tendency for plasticity to saturate, which, in turn, limits the capacity for new learning.
source: Thus, enhanced synaptic plasticity, in the form of a lower threshold for induction, can be opposed by a tendency for plasticity to saturate, which, in turn, limits the capacity for new learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results about the relationship between plasticity threshold and saturation.

claim: The capacity for new learning could be decreased or increased by manipulations that altered activity in the VOR circuit for a few tens of minutes.
source: The capacity for new learning could be decreased or increased by manipulations that altered activity in the VOR circuit for a few tens of minutes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental results showing that 30 minutes of climbing fiber stimulation or behavioral pre-training can alter subsequent learning.

claim: In WT mice, 30 min of elevated climbing-fiber activity induced a state that prevented subsequent learning.
source: In WT mice, 30 min of elevated climbing-fiber activity induced a state that prevented subsequent learning (Figure 2B, CF Stim, solid cyan).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recovery from saturation occurred over a timescale of tens of minutes.
source: Recovery from this saturation also occurred over a timescale of tens of minutes; although VOR-increase learning was profoundly suppressed after climbing fiber stimulation, there was evidence for recovery of learning during the last few minutes of the 30 min training session (Figure 2B, solid blue trace at 30 min), and full recovery a few days later (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 30 min of behavioral pre-training was sufficient to reverse saturation in the DKO mice and transform their learning impairment into a learning enhancement.
source: Likewise, the natural manipulation of circuit activity caused by 30 min of behavioral pre-training was apparently sufficient to reverse saturation in the DKO mice and transform their learning impairment into a learning enhancement (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: If the recent neural activity is appropriately patterned, rapid recovery from saturation is possible, creating the potential for enhanced plasticity to support enhanced learning.
source: Thus, if the recent neural activity is appropriately patterned, rapid recovery from saturation is possible, creating the potential for enhanced plasticity to support enhanced learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that appropriate pre-training can reverse saturation and enable enhanced learning.

claim: The dependence on the recent history of activity may explain the difference between the results from DKO mice in vivo versus in vitro.
source: This dependence on the recent history of activity may explain the difference between the results from DKO mice in vivo versus in vitro. In vitro, the levels of spontaneous activity are much lower than in vivo, hence any saturation that is present in vivo would rapidly decay in vitro, revealing enhancement rather than saturation of pf-Pk LTD (McConnell et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental results and knowledge of differences in activity levels between in vivo and in vitro conditions.

claim: The dependence of learning on the recent history of activity may explain the observation of either impaired or enhanced learning on behavioral tasks that depend on different parts of the cerebellum.
source: The dependence of learning on the recent history of activity may also explain the observation of either impaired or enhanced learning on behavioral tasks that depend on different parts of the cerebellum (McConnell et al., 2009), which have different levels of spontaneous activity (Zhou et al., 2014), and different dependence of LTD induction on the patterns of neural activation (Suvrathan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the current results and citations to previous studies showing regional differences in cerebellar activity and plasticity.

claim: In both DKO and WT mice, the capacity for new learning was highly dependent on the recent history of activity in the circuit over the previous tens of minutes.
source: In sum, in both DKO and WT mice, the capacity for new learning was highly dependent on the recent history of activity in the circuit over the previous tens of minutes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that recent activity (pre-training or climbing fiber stimulation) affects subsequent learning in both genotypes.

claim: Synaptic plasticity and learning are not isomorphic: one cannot predict the learning outcome from the synaptic properties alone.
source: Our findings reinforce the idea that synaptic plasticity and learning are not isomorphic: one cannot predict the learning outcome from the synaptic properties alone.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that the same synaptic manipulation (enhanced LTD) can produce opposite learning outcomes depending on recent activity.

claim: Synaptic plasticity enhancers may be most effective if combined with strategies for controlling basal levels of neural activity.
source: Our results suggest that synaptic plasticity enhancers may be most effective if combined with strategies for controlling basal levels of neural activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about clinical applications based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Suppression of neural activity before training may prime enhanced learning under conditions of enhanced associative plasticity.
source: In particular, suppression of neural activity before training may prime enhanced learning under conditions of enhanced associative plasticity.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about potential therapeutic strategies based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Behavioral therapy could provide an alternative to drugs in patients with pathologically altered synaptic plasticity.
source: In addition, our finding that the appropriate behavioral pre-training can unmask enhanced learning in mice with enhanced synaptic plasticity (Figure 3A) raises the possibility that behavioral therapy could provide an alternative to drugs in patients with pathologically altered synaptic plasticity (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Baudouin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about clinical applications based on inference from the experimental results and citations to previous studies on pathological plasticity.

claim: The finding that the enhancement of synaptic plasticity can result in either enhanced or impaired learning has been reported for many different brain regions, and for both associative LTP and LTD.
source: Yet the finding that the enhancement of synaptic plasticity can result in either enhanced or impaired learning has been reported for many different brain regions, and for both associative LTP and LTD.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature on enhanced plasticity and learning across different brain regions.

claim: Saturation should be considered as a factor that could limit the ability of enhanced plasticity to enhance learning in neural circuits throughout the brain.
source: Therefore, saturation should be considered as a factor that could limit the ability of enhanced plasticity to enhance learning in neural circuits throughout the brain.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings based on inference from the experimental results and knowledge of the literature.

claim: Neural circuits have evolved to optimize the threshold for plasticity to delicately balance the need to prevent inappropriate inputs from triggering and saturating plasticity, while allowing the appropriate inputs to drive learning.
source: One can speculate that in each brain area, neural circuits have evolved to optimize the threshold for plasticity to delicately balance the need to prevent inappropriate inputs from triggering and saturating plasticity, while allowing the appropriate inputs to drive learning.
evidence: The claim is explicitly labeled as speculation about the evolutionary optimization of plasticity thresholds.

claim: Pf-Pk LTD contributes selectively to certain forms of cerebellum-dependent learning and not others.
source: For many years, pf-Pk LTD was widely considered to be the mechanism of all cerebellum-dependent learning (Ito, 2002); however, recent evidence from animals with disrupted pf-Pk LTD suggests it contributes selectively to certain forms of cerebellum-dependent learning and not others (Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006; Titley et al., 2010; Schonewille et al., 2011; Aiba et al., 1994; Shibuki et al., 1996; Endo et al., 2009; Feil et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009; Li et al., 1995; Miyata et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies showing selective contributions of pf-Pk LTD to different forms of learning.

claim: LTD contributes selectively to VOR learning when training to increase the amplitude of the VOR is done using high-frequency (≥1 Hz) visual-vestibular stimuli.
source: Previous work has suggested that LTD contributes selectively to VOR learning when training to increase the amplitude of the VOR is done using high-frequency (≥1 Hz) visual-vestibular stimuli, and much less so, if at all, when VOR learning is tested with other training paradigms (Boyden et al., 2006; Hansel et al., 2006; Titley et al., 2010; Schonewille et al., 2011; Aiba et al., 1994; Shibuki et al., 1996; Endo et al., 2009; Feil et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009; Li et al., 1995; Miyata et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies showing frequency-dependent contributions of LTD to VOR learning.

claim: Mice with enhanced pf-Pk LTD exhibited the same specific VOR learning deficit as mice with impaired pf-Pk LTD.
source: We found that mice with enhanced pf-Pk LTD exhibited the same, specific VOR learning deficit.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similarity of the learning deficit pattern in DKO mice to that previously reported in LTD-impaired mice.

claim: The VOR is an eye movement response to a vestibular stimulus, which functions to stabilize images on the retina during head motion.
source: The VOR is an eye movement response to a vestibular stimulus, which functions to stabilize images on the retina during head motion.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the function of the VOR.

claim: In wild type mice, motor learning can adaptively increase or decrease the amplitude of the VOR to improve image stabilization.
source: In wild type mice, motor learning can adaptively increase or decrease the amplitude of the VOR to improve image stabilization.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about VOR learning in wild type mice.

claim: Classical MHCI H2-Kb and MHCI H2-Db are highly expressed in Purkinje cells in the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, classical MHCI H2-Kb (H2-Kb) and MHCI H2-Db (H2-Db) are highly expressed in Purkinje cells
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the expression pattern of MHCI molecules in the cerebellum.

claim: Climbing-fiber stimulation is known to induce LTD in simultaneously active pf-Pk synapses.
source: Climbing-fiber stimulation is known to induce LTD in simultaneously active pf-Pk synapses (Crepel and Jaillard, 1991; Ekerot and Kano, 1985; Ito and Kano, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies showing that climbing fiber stimulation induces LTD.

claim: During normal VOR learning, climbing fiber activation is thought to induce LTD selectively in those pf-Pk synapses activated by the visual and vestibular stimuli used to induce learning.
source: During normal VOR learning, climbing fiber activation is thought to induce LTD selectively in those pf-Pk synapses activated by the visual and vestibular stimuli used to induce learning.
evidence: The claim is based on established theoretical understanding of how LTD is induced during VOR learning.

claim: Optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation delivered in the absence of visual or vestibular stimuli should induce LTD randomly in spontaneously active pf-Pk synapses.
source: In contrast, optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation delivered in the absence of such stimuli should induce LTD randomly in spontaneously active pf-Pk synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known mechanism of LTD induction and the experimental design.

claim: The normal baseline VOR amplitude in DKO mice is consistent with lesion studies showing normal VOR after flocculus lesions in wild type mice.
source: This is consistent with the normal baseline VOR amplitude in DKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and in wild type mice after lesions of the flocculus (Rambold et al., 2002; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Katoh et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: LTD only increases the amplitude of the VOR if it is induced selectively in the appropriate subset of pf-Pk synapses.
source: Together, these observations indicate that non-specific manipulations of the flocculus are not sufficient to have a coordinated effect on the VOR behavior, and that LTD only increases the amplitude of the VOR if it is induced selectively in the appropriate subset of pf-Pk synapses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: VOR-decrease learning relies on the cerebellar flocculus.
source: Notably, climbing fiber stimulation before training did not perturb subsequent VOR-decrease learning, which also relies on the cerebellar flocculus (Koekkoek et al., 1997; Rambold et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing the role of the flocculus in VOR-decrease learning.

claim: VOR-decrease learning is insensitive to disruptions of pf-Pk LTD.
source: but is insensitive to disruptions of pf-Pk LTD (Boyden et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study showing that VOR-decrease learning is not affected by LTD disruptions.
